svg.title: Built environment equity · Full system
svg.desc: 35 variables and 77 signed relationships. Conceptual model 2026-11-03.2. Signs indicate direction, not desirability.

Income of households facing disadvantage after taxes and transfers, before housing and household energy payments. Assess change for the same households; neighborhood compositional change is V35. Assets and borrowing are contextual buffers, not part of this income flow.

Neighborhood-level effective collective influence over planning, budgets and housing decisions. Influence can favor affluent newcomers; a neighborhood gain is not automatically greater voice for original residents facing disadvantage.
Realized public spending on the focal neighborhood's housing, infrastructure and services. Its equity effect depends on allocation and resident retention.

Institutional effort to prioritize and enact equity-oriented measures in response to monitored needs or health gaps. Distinct from realized spending (V03) and effective housing protections (V05). Detection, mandate, political willingness and implementation are required.
Effective provision and preservation of affordable secure homes, tenant protections and anti-displacement measures for renters and other residents facing housing insecurity or affordability barriers.
Average resources of the resident population; changes may reflect who can afford to enter or remain. A compositional variable, not incumbent household income.
Access for residents facing disadvantage to homes with adequate ventilation, moisture control, thermal comfort and safe materials; energy performance is separately represented.
Energy performance of homes occupied by households facing disadvantage, with adequate ventilation and comfort maintained; implementation costs are not assumed away.

Required household energy expenditure divided by the same household's disposable income over the same period, excluding rent or mortgage payments. Household changes are evaluated before aggregation; zero or negative incomes require separate hardship reporting.

Rent or mortgage payments and mandatory tenure charges divided by the same household's disposable income over the same period; excludes household energy payments. Evaluate a prespecified household-level distribution, not the ratio of unrelated group averages.

Quality-adjusted monthly market rent for comparable dwellings in the focal neighborhood. Actual payments change only for market-exposed tenancies or on a move or renewal. This variable does not represent property asset values or existing fixed mortgage payments.
Market-led neighborhood upgrading and socioeconomic replacement pressure. Effects depend on tenure, timing, safeguards and local institutions.
Uncertainty among residents facing disadvantage about retaining an adequate, affordable home; includes threatened loss and unstable tenure.
Forced or financially compelled residential moves among original residents facing disadvantage; distinct from all residential mobility or cultural change alone.
Connected proximity of everyday destinations and complementary uses. Density alone is deliberately not treated as uniformly beneficial.
Affordable, physically accessible, reliable public transport that meets the destinations and travel needs of residents facing disadvantage; distance to a stop alone is insufficient.
Usable routes, safe crossings, separation and speed management, adapted to age, disability and other access needs.

Walking and cycling time for everyday transport per resident in the defined study group, including walking to public transport. Excludes gym exercise and purely recreational activity. Population coverage, trip purposes and reporting period are fixed.
Reliance on private motorized travel for everyday needs; changing this requires viable alternatives rather than simply restricting mobility.
Motor-vehicle traffic in places used by residents facing disadvantage, with background fleet, road design and speeds held in context.

Condition and usability of shared green spaces serving residents facing disadvantage, including maintenance, welcoming design and effective access. Canopy and shade are separate attributes: a quality improvement has a cooling effect only when it improves those attributes at places people use.
Ability to use affordable, appropriate local services, including healthcare, healthy food and community amenities; includes financial and physical accessibility.
Inclusive trust, support and collective capacity among original residents facing disadvantage; exclusionary bonding is not counted as an equity benefit.
Neglect and environmental disorder of shared places, without treating poverty or demographic composition itself as disorder.
Perceived safety from crime and traffic danger among residents facing disadvantage when using streets and shared places; perceptions may differ from measured risk.

Road-traffic injuries sustained while walking or cycling for transport per resident in the defined study group per year. This is a population incidence measure, not injury risk per trip or per kilometer, and excludes car-occupant-only injuries.
Exposure of residents facing disadvantage to harmful outdoor pollutants. Traffic emissions are one driver; local dispersion and other sources remain contextual.
Harmful environmental noise affecting residents facing disadvantage; unequal exposure is context-dependent rather than assumed in every city.
Harmful heat experienced by residents facing disadvantage, conditional on shade, dwelling conditions, cooling access and individual vulnerability.
Persistent psychosocial stress associated with financial strain, insecurity, environmental conditions and constrained control.
Physical morbidity and functional limitations in residents facing disadvantage. The model represents direction, not a fitted disease incidence rate.
Adverse mental health among residents facing disadvantage, distinguished from stress as a mediating experience; no diagnosis is inferred for individuals.
The ability of working-age residents facing disadvantage to obtain and sustain paid work. The health-to-work link is a synthesis hypothesis sensitive to labor protections.

Percentage-point difference in the prevalence of at least one unmet built-environment need: residents facing disadvantage minus the defined reference group. Agree group-appropriate thresholds for the five stated needs domains before measurement. This proposed non-compensatory indicator is not a validated scale; report each domain alongside it. A positive gap means unmet needs are more common among the residents facing disadvantage.

Percentage-point difference in poor-self-rated-health prevalence: residents facing disadvantage minus the defined reference group, using the same survey definition and period. A positive gap means poor self-rated health is more common among the residents facing disadvantage. Interpreting it as inequity additionally requires an assessment of unfairness and avoidability; physical or mental morbidity does not mechanically determine self-rating.

svg.text: + Same direction − Opposite direction ∥ Delay (duration not estimated)
Solid: source-reported Dashed: inferred / conditional / definition Dotted: disparity indicator
R: reinforcing B: balancing Loop type does not determine benefit or harm.
Conceptual model 2026-11-03.2. Evidence and assumptions: see the interactive atlas.
